candidate.answerReason: There must be two pennies. Comparing the remaining seven coins with seven nickels leaves 65 cents in upgrades; the only allowed combination has three quarters, one dime, and three nickels.

methods.label: Compare the remaining coins with nickels
methods.explanation:
Work in cents. Nickels, dimes, and quarters are worth \(5\), \(10\), and \(25\) cents, so their combined value is a multiple of \(5\). There can be at most \(6\) pennies, because at least three of the nine coins must be the other types. Among \(1\) through \(6\) pennies, only \(2\) pennies leave a multiple of \(5\) when subtracted from \(102\).

Thus the other \(7\) coins total \(100\) cents. Imagine starting with seven nickels, worth \(35\) cents. Replacing a nickel with a dime adds \(5\) cents, and replacing one with a quarter adds \(20\) cents. We need \(100-35=65\) extra cents.

Four quarters would already add \(80\) cents, too much. Since at least one quarter is required, there are just three cases:

- One quarter adds \(20\) cents, leaving \(45\) extra cents, which would require \(9\) dimes. There are too few coins.
- Two quarters add \(40\) cents, leaving \(25\) extra cents, which requires \(5\) dimes. Those seven coins leave no nickel.
- Three quarters add \(60\) cents, leaving \(5\) extra cents, which requires \(1\) dime. The remaining three coins are nickels.

The resulting collection has two pennies, three nickels, one dime, and three quarters. It has nine coins and value
\[
2+15+10+75=102\text{ cents}.
\]
Therefore you must have \(\boxed{1}\) dime, choice A.
methods.levelReason: Multiples of five restrict the pennies, and an elementary comparison with nickels reduces the remaining possibilities to three explicit cases.
